situation:
You and your teammate are the director of national accounts and the director of quality and compliance at HEARTHSTONE PET WORKS, a manufacturer of dog and cat treats, bedding and grooming supplies. The president (judge) has asked the two of you to meet this afternoon about a vendor agreement that is sitting unsigned on the president's desk.

HEARTHSTONE has spent two hard years recovering from a product recall and the loss of its largest distributor. New leadership rebuilt the plant's records, retrained the line crews, and won accounts back by promising that whatever the company puts in writing is exactly what the company does. Employees repeat that promise to one another, and the independent stores that came back say it is the reason they returned.

Last year HEARTHSTONE signed an eighteen-month commitment giving CEDAR CREEK PET CO-OP, a group of independent stores, exclusive retail rights to the company's new grain-free treat line. Last week BRIGHTWAY PET MART, a national chain, offered to launch that same line in more than four hundred of its stores this spring. The order would be the largest the company has shipped since the recall.

BRIGHTWAY's vendor packet includes a supplier statement that must be signed before the order is entered. It certifies that the line reaches no other retail channel and that every unit is produced in facilities HEARTHSTONE owns. Neither line is true today: the co-op commitment still has ten months to run, and part of the treat line is baked at an outside contract plant. The buyer calls the form routine and says the launch window closes Friday.

Signing the statement as written would put a certification in the company's name that HEARTHSTONE's own records contradict, and it would break the commitment the co-op is relying on. Asking BRIGHTWAY to amend the wording could cost the company the order, since the buyer can move the launch to another vendor. Asking the co-op to release the line early would tell the accounts that stayed loyal that their exclusive can be traded away, and the co-op could pull its remaining business.

The president (judge) wants the team to recommend what HEARTHSTONE should do about the order and the supplier statement, how the decision will be explained to the co-op, and what to tell plant employees who are already posting about the possible deal on their personal social media accounts. You will present your recommendation to the president (judge), who will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the president (judge) of HEARTHSTONE PET WORKS. Business background is the same as the situation above. You came in after the recall, rebuilt the company's records, and told every account that what HEARTHSTONE writes down is what HEARTHSTONE does. The BRIGHTWAY order would be the largest since the recall, and the supplier statement in the packet does not match what the co-op commitment and the contract plant make true.

You have asked the director of national accounts and the director of quality and compliance to recommend what the company should do about the BRIGHTWAY order and the supplier statement, how that decision will be explained to CEDAR CREEK PET CO-OP, and what to tell employees who are posting about the deal on their personal accounts.

After the team has presented, ask these questions:
judgeQuestions: Which option did you decide against, and what would it have cost us to take it?
If we had signed the statement the way the buyer wrote it, what would we have had to live with afterward?
